nodes.name: Functional linear regression model
nodes.statement:
Y_i = \int\beta(t) X_i(t) \,dt +
\varepsilon_i, \qquad i = 1,\ldots, n.
nodes.statement_short: Scalar response as integral of a single functional predictor against a coefficient function plus noise.
nodes.label: flin

nodes.name: Centered response and predictors
nodes.statement:
For notational convenience, we assume throughout this paper that the
response and predictors have been centered so the intercept can be
ignored.

nodes.name: Functional additive regression model
nodes.statement:
Y_i = \sum_{j=1}^p
f_j (X_{ij} )+ \varepsilon_i, \qquad i = 1,
\ldots, n,
nodes.statement_short: Response is a sum of p general nonlinear functions of functional predictors plus noise.
nodes.label: far

nodes.name: Sparsity in the predictor space
nodes.statement:
First, in order to make the problem
feasible, we must assume sparsity in the predictor space, that is, that most
of the predictors are unrelated to the response.

nodes.name: Vector of evaluated additive components
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathbf f}_j= (f_j(X_{1j}),\ldots,f_j(X_{nj}) )^T$.

nodes.name: FAR penalized regression criterion
nodes.statement:
Then
our general approach for fitting (\ref{far}) is to minimize the
following penalized regression criterion over ${\mathbf f}_1, {\mathbf f}_2,\ldots,
{\mathbf f}_p$:


\begin{equation} \frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum
_{j=1}^p {\mathbf f}_j \Biggr\Vert
^2_2 + \sum_{j=1}^p
\rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\Vert{\mathbf f}_j\Vert
}_2 \biggr),
\end{equation}

where ${\mathbf Y}=(Y_1,\ldots, Y_n)^T$, $\rho_{\lambda_n}(t)$ is a penalty
function, $\lambda_n$ is the regularization parameter and ${\Vert
{\mathbf f}_j\Vert
}_2=\sqrt{{\mathbf f}_j^T{\mathbf f}_j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fit the additive model by minimizing least squares plus a group penalty on the norms of the component vectors.

nodes.name: FAR optimization criterion
nodes.statement:
\frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum
_{j=1}^p {\mathbf f}_j \Biggr\Vert
^2_2 + \sum_{j=1}^p
\rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\Vert{\mathbf f}_j\Vert
}_2 \biggr),
nodes.statement_short: Penalized least squares over component vectors with penalty applied to scaled norms.
nodes.label: fundamental

nodes.name: Euclidean norm notation
nodes.statement:
To aid the presentation, we drop the
subscript and use $\Vert \cdot\Vert $ to denote the $\ell_2$ norm
of a vector
in the future.

nodes.name: l1 (Lasso) penalty
nodes.statement:
In this article, we explore
general concave functions for $\rho$, with the $\ell_1$ penalty $\rho
_{\lambda}(t) = \lambda t$ considered as a special case.

nodes.name: Fully observed trajectories
nodes.statement:
We assume that the trajectories of functional predictors, $X_{ij}(t)$,
are fully observed.

nodes.name: Single index model
nodes.statement:
For a centered
response, the standard single index model can be expressed in the form
$Y=g({\bolds\beta}^T{\mathbf X}) + \varepsilon$,
where $g(x)$ is a general
nonlinear function and ${\bolds\beta}$ is a norm one vector representing the
best single direction to project the predictors into.
nodes.statement_short: Response is a nonlinear link of a single norm-one linear projection of the predictors.

nodes.name: Functional single index model
nodes.statement:
Index models can be naturally extended to
functional predictors using the formulation $f_j(X_{ij}) = g_j
(\int\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt )$, where $g_j(x)$ and $\beta_j(t)$
are both nonparametric smooth functions, and the integral is
well-defined.
nodes.origin_citation: James and Silverman 2005; Amato et al. 2006; Chen, Hall and Muller 2011
nodes.statement_short: Component f_j is a smooth link g_j of the integral of the predictor against an index function.

nodes.name: Nonlinear FAR model (functional single index form)
nodes.statement:
Y_i = \sum_{j=1}^p
g_j \biggl(\int\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt \biggr)
+ \varepsilon_i.
nodes.statement_short: FAR model with each component a single-index link of a functional projection.
nodes.label: simfar

nodes.name: Centering of regression functions for identifiability
nodes.statement:
For identifiability, in addition to centering the response, we also
center the regression functions: $\sum_{i=1}^n g_j (\int\beta
_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt )=0$ for all~$j$.

nodes.name: Index functions identifiable only up to scaling
nodes.statement:
Note that index functions
$\beta_j$ are only identifiable up to multiplications by nonzero
constants, however, our focus is on estimating $f_j$ rather than $\beta
_j$.

nodes.name: General nonlinear FAR optimization criterion
nodes.statement:
\frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum
_{j=1}^p g_j \biggl(\int
\beta_j(t) {\mathbf X}_j(t)\,dt \biggr)\Biggr\Vert
^2 + \sum_{j=1}^p
\rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\Vert{\mathbf f}_j\Vert
\biggr),
nodes.label: nonlinfar

nodes.name: Observation range [0,1]
nodes.statement:
We assume without loss of generality that each predictor is observed
over the range $0\le t \le1$.

nodes.name: Linear additive component
nodes.statement:
f_j(X_{ij}) = \int_0^1
\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt,
nodes.label: linearf

nodes.name: Linear FAR optimization criterion
nodes.statement:
\frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum
_{j=1}^p \int_0^1
\beta_j(t) {\mathbf X}_j(t)\,dt\Biggr\Vert^2 +
\sum_{j=1}^p \rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(
\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert{\mathbf f}_j\Vert\biggr),
nodes.label: linearfar

nodes.name: Orthonormal basis expansions of predictors and coefficients
nodes.statement:
X_{ij}(t) = \sum_{l=1}^\infty
\theta_{ijl}b_l(t), \qquad\beta_j(t) = \sum
_{l=1}^\infty\eta_{0,jl}b_l(t),
nodes.label: eqbasis-rep

nodes.name: Basis representation of linear additive component
nodes.statement:
f_j(X_{ij}) = \int_0^1
X_{ij}(t)\beta_j(t)\,dt = \sum_{l=1}^\infty
\theta_{ijl}\eta_{0,jl}.
nodes.label: fexpan

nodes.name: Truncated basis coefficient vectors
nodes.statement:
Specifically, for a given sequence of integers $q_n = o(n)$ depending
only on the sample size $n$, write $\bolds\eta_{0j} = (\eta_{0,j1},\ldots
,\eta_{0,jq_n})^T$ and $\bolds\theta_{ij} = (\theta_{ij1},\ldots, \theta
_{ijq_n})^T$.

nodes.name: Basis approximation error
nodes.statement:
Denote by $e_{ij}$ the
approximation error, that is,


\begin{equation} e_{ij} = f_j(X_{ij})-
\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{0j} = \sum
_{l=q_n+1}^\infty\theta_{ijl}\eta_{0,jl}.
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Approximation error definition
nodes.statement:
e_{ij} = f_j(X_{ij})-
\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{0j} = \sum
_{l=q_n+1}^\infty\theta_{ijl}\eta_{0,jl}.
nodes.label: deferr

nodes.name: Uniform bound on the basis approximation error
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz with the Sobolev condition gives |e_ij|^2 = O(q_n^{-4}).
nodes.label: eqapp-err

nodes.name: Basis coefficient matrix Theta_j
nodes.statement:
Let $\Theta_j$ be an
$n\times q_n$ matrix whose rows are formed by $\{\bolds\theta_{ij},
i=1,\ldots, n\}$.

nodes.name: Approximate linear FAR criterion (group penalized)
nodes.statement:
\frac{1}{2n}\Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}- \sum
_{j=1}^p\Theta_j\bolds\eta_j
\Biggr\Vert^2+\sum_{j=1}^p
\rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert\Theta_j
\bolds\eta_j\Vert\biggr).
nodes.statement_short: Finite-dimensional group-penalized least squares in basis coefficients.
nodes.label: newopt2

nodes.name: Linear FAR fitting problem
nodes.statement:
Hence, we fit FAR by minimizing
(\ref{newopt2}) over $\bolds\eta_1,\ldots, \bolds\eta_p$.

nodes.name: Closed-form coordinate update for the Lasso penalty
nodes.statement:
If $\rho_{\lambda_n}(t) = \lambda_nt$, then the solution to (\ref
{newopt2}) satisfies $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j = \Theta_j\hat{\bolds\eta}_j$

where

\[
\hat{\bolds\eta}_j = \biggl(1-\frac{\sqrt{n}\lambda_n}{\Vert S_j{\mathbf R}_j\Vert
} \biggr)_+\bigl(
\Theta_j^T \Theta_j\bigr)^{-1}
\Theta_j^T{\mathbf R}_j,
\]

$S_j = \Theta_j(\Theta_j^T\Theta_j)^{-1}\Theta_j^T$, ${\mathbf R}_j = {\mathbf Y}
- \sum_{k\neq j}\Theta_k\hat{\bolds\eta}_k$, and $z_+ = \max(0,z)$
represents the positive part of $z$.
nodes.statement_short: With the l1 penalty, each block minimizer is a group soft-thresholded projection of the partial residual.
nodes.label: propL1

nodes.name: Linear FAR algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Block coordinate descent: project the partial residual onto each predictor's basis, group soft-threshold, center, cycle to convergence.
nodes.label: alglin

nodes.name: Monotone decrease of the criterion
nodes.statement:
In addition, it is clear from
Proposition~\ref{propL1} that
(\ref{newopt2}) will decrease at each step.

nodes.name: FAR algorithm for general penalties via local linear approximation
nodes.statement:
For a general penalty function, $\rho_{\lambda_n}(t)$, we use the
local linear approximation method proposed in \cite{ZL08} to solve
(\ref{newopt2}). The penalty function can be approximated as $\rho
_{\lambda_n}(\Vert {\mathbf f}\Vert /\sqrt
n)\approx
\rho'_{\lambda_n}(\Vert {\mathbf f}^*\Vert /\sqrt n)\Vert {\mathbf f}
\Vert /\sqrt n+C$, where
${\mathbf f}^*$ is some vector that is close to ${\mathbf f}$ and $C=\rho_{\lambda
_n}(\Vert {\mathbf f}^*\Vert /\sqrt
n)-\rho_{\lambda_n}'(\Vert {\mathbf f}^*\Vert /\sqrt n)\Vert {\mathbf f}
^*\Vert /\sqrt n$ is a
constant. Hence, the only required change to the FAR algorithm for
optimizing over general penalty
functions is to replace the calculation of $\alpha_j$ in step~3 by

\[
\alpha_j = \biggl(1-\rho'_{\lambda_n}\biggl(
\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j\Vert\biggr)\sqrt n/\Vert\widehat
{\mathbf P}_j\Vert\biggr)_+,
\]

where $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j$ represents the most recent estimate for ${\mathbf f}_j$. The
initial estimate of $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j$ can be obtained by using the Lasso
penalty.
nodes.statement_short: Local linear approximation of a concave penalty turns each update into a reweighted group soft-threshold, initialized at the Lasso fit.

nodes.name: Linearize the penalty
nodes.statement:
The penalty function can be approximated as $\rho
_{\lambda_n}(\Vert {\mathbf f}\Vert /\sqrt
n)\approx
\rho'_{\lambda_n}(\Vert {\mathbf f}^*\Vert /\sqrt n)\Vert {\mathbf f}
\Vert /\sqrt n+C$, where
${\mathbf f}^*$ is some vector that is close to ${\mathbf f}$ and $C=\rho_{\lambda
_n}(\Vert {\mathbf f}^*\Vert /\sqrt
n)-\rho_{\lambda_n}'(\Vert {\mathbf f}^*\Vert /\sqrt n)\Vert {\mathbf f}
^*\Vert /\sqrt n$ is a
constant.
nodes.statement_short: Local linear approximation of the penalty around a nearby f*.

nodes.name: Replace shrinkage factor
nodes.statement:
Hence, the only required change to the FAR algorithm for
optimizing over general penalty
functions is to replace the calculation of $\alpha_j$ in step~3 by

\[
\alpha_j = \biggl(1-\rho'_{\lambda_n}\biggl(
\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j\Vert\biggr)\sqrt n/\Vert\widehat
{\mathbf P}_j\Vert\biggr)_+,
\]

where $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j$ represents the most recent estimate for ${\mathbf f}_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Use derivative-weighted shrinkage factor in step 3.

nodes.name: Lasso initialization
nodes.statement:
The
initial estimate of $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j$ can be obtained by using the Lasso
penalty.
nodes.statement_short: Initialize with the Lasso-penalized fit.

nodes.name: Unit-norm index functions
nodes.statement:
Since
$\beta_j(t)$ corresponds to a direction that we project $X_{ij}(t)$
into we impose the constraint $\Vert \beta_j\Vert _2=1$.

nodes.name: Basis approximation of link functions
nodes.statement:
We assume that $g_j(x)$ can be well
approximated by a $d_n$-dimensional basis ${\mathbf h}(x)$ such that $g_j(x)
\approx
{\mathbf h}(x)^T \bolds\xi_j$.

nodes.name: Nonlinear FAR criterion in basis form
nodes.statement:
\frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum
_{j=1}^p H_j\bolds\xi_j\Biggr
\Vert^2 + \sum_{j=1}^p
\rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\Vert H_j
\bolds\xi_j\Vert\biggr),
nodes.label: nonlinfar2

nodes.name: Sum of squares for index estimation
nodes.statement:
\sum_{i=1}^n
\Biggl(Y_i-\sum_{j=1}^p{\mathbf h}
\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T \bolds\eta_j
\bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j \Biggr)^2
nodes.label: etaopt

nodes.name: Nonlinear FAR algorithm
nodes.statement:
\caption{\textbf{Nonlinear FAR algorithm}} \begin{enumerate}

\item[0.] Initialize\vspace*{2pt}~$\hat{\bolds\eta}_j$ for $j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$
using the linear FAR algorithm.




\item[1.] Compute $\widehat H_j$ using the current estimates for $\bolds\eta_j$.

\item[2.] Estimate $\bolds\xi_j$ for $j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$ by minimizing
(\ref{nonlinfar2}) given the current values of $\widehat H_j$.

\item[3.] Conditional on the $\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$'s from step~2, estimate the
$\bolds\eta_j$'s by minimizing (\ref{etaopt}).

\item[4.] Repeat steps 1~through 3 and iterate until convergence.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Alternate between penalized estimation of link coefficients (via linear FAR) and least-squares re-estimation of index directions.
nodes.label: algnonlin

nodes.name: Equivalence of criteria for fixed H_j
nodes.statement:
One of the appealing aspects of this approach is that, for fixed $\widehat
H_j$, (\ref{newopt2}) and (\ref{nonlinfar2}) are equivalent so
estimation of the $\bolds\xi_j$'s in step 2 can be achieved using the
linear FAR algorithm from Section~\ref{seclinearfar}.

nodes.name: Efficient nonlinear FAR tuning path
nodes.statement:
However, we have found that a more efficient
approach is to compute initial estimates for $\bolds\eta_j$, minimize
(\ref{nonlinfar2}) over $\bolds\xi_j$ for each possible value of $\lambda
$, choose the $\bolds\xi_j$'s corresponding to the ``best'' value of
$\lambda$, estimate the $\bolds\eta_j$'s for only this one set of
parameters, and iterate.
nodes.statement_short: Fit the link coefficients over the whole lambda grid, pick the best lambda, update index directions only for it, and iterate.

nodes.name: Initial index estimates
nodes.statement: compute initial estimates for $\bolds\eta_j$
nodes.statement_short: Initialize index vectors.

nodes.name: Path over lambda
nodes.statement:
minimize
(\ref{nonlinfar2}) over $\bolds\xi_j$ for each possible value of $\lambda
$
nodes.statement_short: Solve the penalized problem for every lambda.

nodes.name: Choose best lambda
nodes.statement:
choose the $\bolds\xi_j$'s corresponding to the ``best'' value of
$\lambda$
nodes.statement_short: Select the best lambda.

nodes.name: Re-estimate index
nodes.statement:
estimate the $\bolds\eta_j$'s for only this one set of
parameters
nodes.statement_short: Update index directions for the chosen lambda only.

nodes.name: Degrees of freedom of the Lasso
nodes.statement:
For the Lasso, it has been
shown that an unbiased estimate for this quantity is the number of
nonzero coefficients \cite{zou2}.
conclusions:
an unbiased estimate for this quantity is the number of
nonzero coefficients

nodes.name: Effective degrees of freedom for FAR
nodes.statement:
Computing the effective degrees of
freedom for FAR is a topic for future research.

nodes.name: True predictor set M_0 and sparsity s_n
nodes.statement:
Denote by $\mathfrak{M}_0 = \{j: \beta_j(t)\neq0, 1\leq j\leq p\}$ the set
of true functional predictors and let $s_n$ represent the cardinality
of $\mathfrak{M}_0$.

nodes.name: True coefficient vector eta_0
nodes.statement:
Let $\bolds\eta_0 =
(\bolds\eta_{0,1}, \ldots, \bolds\eta_{0,p}) \in R^{pq_n}$ with $\bolds\eta
_{0j}$ representing the true coefficient vector in the basis
representation $f_j(X_{ij}) = \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{0j} + e_{ij}$.

nodes.name: Stacked subvectors and submatrices
nodes.statement:
For\vspace*{1pt} any index set $S \subset\{1,\ldots, p\}$, we use $\bolds\eta_S$ to
denote the vector formed by stacking vectors $\bolds\eta_j$, $j\in S$ one
underneath each other, and
$\Theta_S$ to denote the matrix formed by stacking the matrices
$\Theta_j$, $j\in S$ one after another.

nodes.name: Column standardization of Theta
nodes.statement:
Moreover, we standardize each
column of $\Theta$ such that they all have $\ell_2$-norm $\sqrt{n}$.

nodes.name: Oracle model selection property of linear FAR
nodes.statement:
Assume that $q_n + \log p = O(n\lambda_n^2)
$, $\lambda_n n^{\alpha}q_n\sqrt{s_n} \rightarrow0$, and $\log
(pq_n) = o(n^{1-2\alpha}s_n^{-1}q_n^{-2})$ with $\alpha$ defined in
Condition~\ref{as2}\textup{(B)}. Further assume that $s_nq_n^{-2} = o(\lambda
_n)$, then under Conditions~\ref{as3} and~\ref{as2}, with probability
tending to 1 as $ n
\rightarrow\infty$, there exists a local minimizer $\hat{\bolds\eta}$ of
(\ref{newopt2}) such that:

\begin{longlist}[(2)]

\item[(1)] $\hat{\bolds\eta}_{\mathfrak{M}_0^c}=0$,

\item[(2)] $\Vert \hat{\bolds\eta}_{\mathfrak{M}_0} - \bolds\eta_{0\mathfrak{M}_0}\Vert
_\infty\leq
c_0^{1/2}n^{-\alpha}q_n^{-1/2}$,
\end{longlist}

where $\Vert \cdot\Vert _\infty$ stands for the infinity norm of
a vector.
nodes.statement_short: With probability tending to one a local minimizer excludes all noise predictors and estimates signal coefficients at rate n^{-alpha} in sup norm.
nodes.label: T2

nodes.name: Local minimizers within statistical precision
nodes.statement:
Although Theorem~\ref{T2} is on a local minimizer of the linear FAR
criterion (\ref{newopt2}), it has been proved by \cite{loh13} that
any local minimizer will fall within statistical precision of the true
parameter vector under appropriate conditions on the penalty function.

nodes.name: Estimated and true component vectors
nodes.statement:
Denote by $\hat{\mathbf f}_j = \Theta_j\hat{\bolds\eta}_j$ and ${\mathbf f}_{0j} =
(f_j(X_{j1}), \ldots, f_j(X_{jn}))^T$, respectively, the estimated and
true values of the $j$th functional
component, both evaluated at the $n$ training data points.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement:
Then the
corollary below follows immediately from Theorem~\ref{T2} and
Condition~\ref{as3}.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from Theorem 1 and the basis approximation condition.

nodes.name: Selection and estimation bound for FAR component functions
nodes.statement:
Suppose the conditions in Theorem~\ref
{T2} are satisfied. Then with probability tending to 1 as $n\rightarrow
\infty$, there exists a FAR
estimate such that $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j = 0$ for $j\notin\mathfrak{M}_0$, and

\[
\max_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j -
{\mathbf f}_{0j}\Vert_2 \leq C_2n^{-\alpha},
\]








where $C_2$ is some positive constant.
assumptions:
Suppose the conditions in Theorem~\ref
{T2} are satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Noise components are estimated as zero and signal components converge at rate n^{-alpha} in empirical l2.
nodes.label: cor1

nodes.name: Asymptotic normality of linear FAR estimator
nodes.statement:
Assume that the conditions in Theorem~\ref{T2} hold and in addition,
$\rho_{\lambda_n}'(a_n/2)=o(a_nn^{\alpha-\sfrac{1}{2}}s_n^{-1/2})$,
$\sup_{t\geq\sfrac{a_n}{2}}\rho_{\lambda_n}''(t)=O(n^{-1/2})$,
$s_{n}=o(n^{2\alpha})$ and $s_nq_n^{-2} = o(n^{-1/2})$. Then with
probability tending to 1
as $n \rightarrow\infty$, there exists a strict local minimizer
$\hat{\bolds\eta}$
of (\ref{newopt2}) such that $\hat{\bolds\eta}_{\mathfrak{M}_0^c} = 0$ and

\[
{\mathbf c}^T \bigl[\bigl(\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T
\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}\bigr)^{1/2}(\hat{\bolds\eta}_{\mathfrak{M}_0} -
\bolds\eta_{0,\mathfrak{M}_0}) + n\bigl(\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T\Theta
_{\mathfrak{M}_0}\bigr)^{-1/2}{\mathbf v}_{0,\mathfrak{M}_0}\bigr] \stackrel{\mathscr{D}}{\longrightarrow} N\bigl(0,
\sigma^2\bigr), 
\]

where ${\mathbf c}\in\mathbf{R}^{q_ns_n}$ satisfies ${\mathbf c}^T{\mathbf c}= 1$ and
${\mathbf v}_{0,\mathfrak{M}_0}$ is a vector formed by stacking the
vectors
${\mathbf v}_{0,k}=\rho'_{\lambda_n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert \Theta_k \bolds\eta
_{0,k}\Vert )\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \frac{\Theta_k^T\Theta_k\bolds\eta
_{0,k}}{\Vert \Theta_k\bolds\eta_{0,k}\Vert }$,
$k\in\mathfrak{M}_0$ underneath each other.
nodes.statement_short: A strict local minimizer is sparse and its signal coefficients, after bias correction, are asymptotically normal.
assumptions: Assume that the conditions in Theorem~\ref{T2} hold
conclusions:
there exists a strict local minimizer
$\hat{\bolds\eta}$
of (\ref{newopt2}) such that $\hat{\bolds\eta}_{\mathfrak{M}_0^c} = 0$
nodes.label: T3

nodes.name: Projected values at a new observation
nodes.statement:
Let $f_{0j}^* = {\bolds\theta_j^*}^T\bolds\eta_{0j}$ and $\hat f_{j}^* =
{\bolds\theta^*_j}^T\hat{\bolds\eta}_{j}$, with $\bolds\theta_j^*\in R^{q_n}$ the
coefficient vector when projecting a given
new observation, $X^*_j(t)$, onto the basis function, $\mathbf{b}(t)$.

nodes.name: Stacked vectors f_0^* and hat f^*
nodes.statement:
Define ${\mathbf f}_0^* = (f_{01}^*, \ldots, f_{0p}^*)^T$ and $\hat{{\mathbf f}}^* =
(\hat f_1^*, \ldots, \hat f_p^*)^T$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2
nodes.statement:
Taking ${\mathbf c}=
(\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0})^{-1/2}\Theta^*\tilde{\mathbf c}
_0$ with $\Theta^* = \operatorname{diag} ({\bolds\theta_1^*}, \ldots,
{\bolds\theta_{s_n}^*} )\in R^{(q_ns_n) \times s_n}$
in Theorem~\ref{T3} and $\tilde{\mathbf c}_0$ a vector in $R^{s_n}$, we have
the following asymptotic normality of ${\mathbf f}_0^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize Theorem 2 to the contrast vector c built from the new-observation basis coefficients.

nodes.name: Asymptotic normality of FAR predictions at a new observation
nodes.statement:
Assume that the conditions in Theorem~\ref{T3} hold.
Then with probability tending to 1
as $n \rightarrow\infty$, there exists a FAR estimate such that
$\hat{{\mathbf f}}_{\mathfrak{M}_0^c}^* = 0$. Moreover,

\[
\tilde{\mathbf c}^T_0\bigl[\hat{{\mathbf f}}_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^* -
{\mathbf f}_{0,\mathfrak{M}_0}^* + n\bigl(\Theta^*\bigr)^T\bigl(
\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}\bigr)^{-1}
{\mathbf v}_{0,\mathfrak{M}
_0}\bigr]\stackrel{\mathscr{D}}{\longrightarrow} N\bigl(0, \sigma^2\bigr),
\]

where $\tilde{\mathbf c}_0$ is a vector in $R^{s_n}$ satisfying $\tilde{\mathbf c}
_0^T(\Theta^*)^T(\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0})^{-1}\Theta
^*\tilde{\mathbf c}_0 = 1$, and ${\mathbf v}_{0,\mathfrak{M}_0}$
is defined in Theorem~\ref{T3}.
assumptions: Assume that the conditions in Theorem~\ref{T3} hold.
conclusions:
there exists a FAR estimate such that
$\hat{{\mathbf f}}_{\mathfrak{M}_0^c}^* = 0$
nodes.statement_short: Bias-corrected predicted component values at a new observation are asymptotically normal.

nodes.name: l1 penalty in nonlinear theory
nodes.statement:
Throughout this section, we focus on the minimizer of the nonlinear
FAR criterion with the $\ell_1$ penalty function.

nodes.name: Deterministic predictors
nodes.statement:
We treat all the
predictors as deterministic.

nodes.name: Centered true regression functions and response
nodes.statement:
For identifiability purposes, we assume
that the true regression functions, $f_{0j}$, as well as the response
vector, are centered, that is, $\sum_{i=1}^n f_{0j}(X_{ij})=0$ and
$\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i=0$.

nodes.name: Cubic B-spline approximation of link functions
nodes.statement: We use cubic B-splines to approximate the true ``link'' functions, $g_{0j}$.

nodes.name: B-spline basis for candidate link
nodes.statement:
Given a candidate index vector $\bolds\eta_j$, the B-spline basis for
representing a candidate link function for the $j$th predictor is
constructed using uniformly placed knots on the interval $[\min_i
\bolds\eta^T_j\bolds\theta_{ij},\max_i \bolds\eta^T_j\bolds\theta_{ij}]$. The
corresponding row vector valued basis function is denoted by~${\mathbf h}
_{\bolds\eta_j,j}$.

nodes.name: Class of candidate regression functions
Empirical l2 distance
nodes.statement:
If~$\tilde f$ and~$\check{f}$ belong
to~${\mathcal F}_j^0$, we denote by $\Vert \tilde f-\check{f}\Vert _n$ the $\ell_2$
distance between these two functions with respect to the empirical
probability measure corresponding to $\bolds\theta_{1j},\ldots,\bolds\theta
_{nj}$. More specifically, $\Vert \tilde f-\check{f}\Vert
^2_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (\tilde f(\bolds\theta_{ij})- \check{f}(\bolds\theta
_{ij}))^2$.

nodes.name: Estimated regression function
True regression functions f_{0j}
nodes.statement:
The\vspace*{1pt}
corresponding true regression functions are referred to as $f_{0j}$.

nodes.name: Empirical distance between estimate and truth
nodes.statement:
We
slightly abuse the notation and write $\Vert \hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert _n$ for
the $\ell_2$ distance between $\hat f_j$ and $f_{0j}$ with respect to
the empirical probability measure corresponding to the $j$th predictor:

\begin{eqnarray*}
\Vert\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert^2_n&=&
\frac{1}n\sum_{i=1}^n \bigl[
\hat f_j(\bolds\theta_{ij})- f_{0j}(X_{ij})
\bigr]^2
\\
&=&\frac{1}n\sum_{i=1}^n \biggl[
\hat g_j \bigl(\hat{\bolds\eta}_j^T
\bolds\theta_{ij} \bigr)- g_{0j} \biggl(\int_0^1
\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt \biggr) \biggr]^2.
\end{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: Signal index set (nonlinear setting)
nodes.statement:
As before, we write~$\mathfrak{M}_0$ for the index set of the signal
predictors, that is, $\mathfrak{M}_0 =\{j: 1\le j\le{p_n}, f_{0j}\ne0\}$.

nodes.name: Universal constant
nodes.statement:
A
\textit{universal constant} is interpreted as a constant that does not
depend on~$n$ or any of the other parameters that appear in the
corresponding expression.

nodes.name: Asymptotic inequality notation
nodes.statement:
Given expressions~$E_1$ and~$E_2$, we
use~$E_1\gtrsim E_2$ to mean that there exists a positive universal
constant~$c$, such that $E_1\ge cE_2$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic equivalence notation
nodes.statement:
We write $E_1\asymp E_2$ when
both $E_1\gtrsim E_2$ and $E_2\gtrsim E_1$ are satisfied.

nodes.name: Rate of convergence of nonlinear FAR
nodes.statement:
Suppose that Conditions~\ref{cond3} and~\ref{as4} are satisfied. Let
$q_n\gtrsim d_n\gtrsim\log\log n$. Then there exists a universal
constant $c$, such that for $\lambda_n\ge
c(n^{-1/2}q_n^{1/2}+n^{-1/2}\sqrt{\log{p_n}})$, the following bound
holds with probability tending to one, as $n$ tends to infinity:


\begin{equation} \sum_{j=1}^{{p_n}} \Vert
\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert_n= O
\bigl(s_n\lambda_n+s_nd_n^{-2}+s_n^2n^{1/2}d_n^{-4}q_n^{-1/2}
\bigr).
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: With lambda_n of order sqrt((q_n+log p_n)/n), the summed empirical l2 error of the nonlinear FAR components is O(s_n lambda_n + approximation terms).
assumptions: Suppose that Conditions~\ref{cond3} and~\ref{as4} are satisfied.
conclusions:
the following bound
holds with probability tending to one, as $n$ tends to infinity:
nodes.label: nonlinthm

nodes.name: Nonlinear FAR error bound
nodes.statement:
\sum_{j=1}^{{p_n}} \Vert
\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert_n= O
\bigl(s_n\lambda_n+s_nd_n^{-2}+s_n^2n^{1/2}d_n^{-4}q_n^{-1/2}
\bigr).
nodes.label: nonlinthmbnd

nodes.name: Case q_n/d_n = o(1) gives inferior bound
nodes.statement:
Note that the case
$q_n/d_n=o(1)$ is not covered in the statement of Theorem~\ref
{nonlinthm}. However, it follows from the proof of the theorem that
such settings correspond to an error bound that is inferior to the one
presented below.

nodes.name: Optimal rate for nonlinear FAR
nodes.statement:
Suppose that Conditions~\ref{cond3} and~\ref{as4} are satisfied. Let
$q_n\asymp d_n\asymp(s_nn)^{1/5}$. Then\vspace*{1pt} there exists a universal
constant $c$, such that for $\lambda_n \ge
c(s_n^{1/10}n^{-2/5}+n^{-1/2}\sqrt{\log{p_n}})$, the following bound
holds with probability tending to one, as $n$ tends to infinity:

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{{p_n}} \Vert\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert_n= O(s_n
\lambda_n).
\]
nodes.statement_short: Choosing q_n and d_n of order (s_n n)^{1/5} yields summed error O(s_n lambda_n).
assumptions: Suppose that Conditions~\ref{cond3} and~\ref{as4} are satisfied.
conclusions:
the following bound
holds with probability tending to one, as $n$ tends to infinity:
nodes.label: nonlinratecor

nodes.name: Thresholded FAR estimator
nodes.statement:
We
define the thresholded FAR estimator as follows: $\tilde f_j=\hat f_j I{\{\Vert \hat f_j\Vert _n> \lambda_n\}}$,
$j=1,\ldots
,p_n$.

nodes.name: Selected index set after thresholding
nodes.statement:
Let~$\widetilde\mathfrak{M}_n$ denote
the index set of the corresponding nonzero regression function
estimates, $\{j: 1\le j\le{p_n}, \tilde f_{j}\ne0\}$.

nodes.name: Error bound and model size of thresholded FAR
nodes.statement:
Under\vspace*{1pt} the assumptions of Corollary~\ref{nonlinratecor}, there exists
a universal constant $c$, such that for $\lambda_n \ge
c(s_n^{1/10}n^{-2/5}+n^{-1/2}\sqrt{\log{p_n}})$, the following bounds
hold with probability tending to one, as $n$ tends to infinity:

\begin{eqnarray*}
\vert\widetilde\mathfrak{M}_n\vert &=& O(s_n)\quad
\mbox{and}
\\
\sum_{j=1}^{{p_n}} \Vert\tilde f_j-f_{0j}\Vert_n &=& O(s_n
\lambda_n).
\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Thresholded FAR selects O(s_n) predictors and keeps summed error O(s_n lambda_n).
conclusions:
the following bounds
hold with probability tending to one, as $n$ tends to infinity:
nodes.label: threshthm

nodes.name: No false negatives and bounded false positives
nodes.statement:
Now consider the case where the components of the FAR model do not
depend on~$n$. More specifically, suppose that the number of signal
predictors, $\vert \mathfrak{M}_0\vert $, and the signal regression
functions, $\{
f_{0k}\}_{k\in\mathfrak{M}_0}$, are fixed and do not change with~$n$. The
estimation error bound in Theorem~\ref{threshthm} implies that, with
probability tending to one, our estimator has zero false negatives,
while the number of false positives stays bounded.
assumptions:
suppose that the number of signal
predictors, $\vert \mathfrak{M}_0\vert $, and the signal regression
functions, $\{
f_{0k}\}_{k\in\mathfrak{M}_0}$, are fixed and do not change with~$n$.
conclusions:
our estimator has zero false negatives,
while the number of false positives stays bounded

nodes.name: Exact support recovery by thresholded FAR
nodes.statement:
Suppose that the components of the FAR model do not depend on~$n$.
Suppose also that the assumptions of Corollary~\ref{nonlinratecor}
are satisfied. Then there exist universal constants~$\tau_0$ and~$c$,
such that, provided $\tau\ge\tau_0$, $\lambda_n \ge
c(s_n^{1/10}n^{-2/5}+n^{-1/2}\sqrt{\log{p_n}})$ and $\lambda
_n=o(1)$, we have

\[
\widetilde\mathfrak{M}_n=\mathfrak{M}_0,
\]

with probability tending to one, as~$n$ goes to infinity.
nodes.statement_short: With fixed model components and a large enough threshold multiple, thresholded FAR recovers the true predictor set.
assumptions: Suppose that the components of the FAR model do not depend on~$n$.

Suppose also that the assumptions of Corollary~\ref{nonlinratecor}
are satisfied.
nodes.label: threshcor

nodes.name: Initialization and index-update details of nonlinear FAR
nodes.statement:
In the initialization step (step~0) of this algorithm, some of the
$\bolds\eta_j$'s will likely be set to zero. This suggests that the
corresponding predictors do not appear related to the response.
However, the initialization assumes a linear model. It is conceivable
that a response that appears unimportant using a linear model will
become statistically significant using a nonlinear model. Hence, if
$\bolds\eta_j$ is estimated to be zero in step~0 we instead set $\bolds\eta
_j$ equal to the loading vector of the first principal component of
$\Theta_j$. This estimate is the direction that explains the most
variability in $X_{ij}(t)$ so is the most natural unsupervised
projection and allows for potential nonlinear relationships to be
detected in step~2.

To implement step~3 of the FAR algorithm, we minimize (\ref{etaopt})
with respect to the $\bolds\eta_j$'s. Directly minimizing (\ref{etaopt})
is difficult due to the nonlinearity of the functions $g_j(t)\approx
{\mathbf h}(t)^T\bolds\xi_j$. To overcome this difficulty, we observe that, with
the estimate $\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$ from step~2 and the current value $\bolds\eta
_{j,\mathrm{old}}$ of $\bolds\eta_j$, the first-order approximation of $g(\bolds\theta
_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j)\approx{\mathbf h}(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$ is


\begin{equation} \qquad{\mathbf h}\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j
\bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j\approx{\mathbf h}\bigl(\bolds\theta
_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}\bigr)^T
\hat{\bolds\xi}_j + {\mathbf h}'\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T
\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}\bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j \cdot
\bolds\theta_{ij}^T(\bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}).
\end{equation}

Thus, we can approximate (\ref{etaopt}) as


\begin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^n
\Biggl(R_i - \sum_{j=1}^p
{\mathbf h}'\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}
\bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j \cdot\bolds\theta_{ij}^T(
\bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}) \Biggr)^2,
\end{equation}

where\vspace*{1pt} $R_i = Y_i - \sum_{j=1}^p {\mathbf h}(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta
_{j,\mathrm{old}})^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j $, that is, the residual for the $i$th observation
from step~2 of the algorithm in the current iteration. The above
approximation (\ref{etaoptapprox}) is a quadratic function of $\bolds\eta
_j$ and can be minimized easily. Hence, the new value of $\bolds\eta_j$ is
updated as the minimizer of (\ref{etaoptapprox}). We also note that if
the estimate $\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$ from step~2 is $\mathbf{0}$, then the
corresponding value of $\bolds\eta_j$ will not be updated.
nodes.section: A Details of the nonlinear FAR algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Replace zero initial index vectors by the first principal component loading, and update index vectors by minimizing a first-order Taylor linearization of the sum of squares.

nodes.statement:
Hence, if
$\bolds\eta_j$ is estimated to be zero in step~0 we instead set $\bolds\eta

To overcome this difficulty, we observe that, with
the estimate $\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$ from step~2 and the current value $\bolds\eta
_{j,\mathrm{old}}$ of $\bolds\eta_j$, the first-order approximation of $g(\bolds\theta

\begin{equation} \qquad{\mathbf h}\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j
\bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j\approx{\mathbf h}\bigl(\bolds\theta

\hat{\bolds\xi}_j + {\mathbf h}'\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T
\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}\bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j \cdot
\bolds\theta_{ij}^T(\bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}).
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: First-order Taylor expansion of the fitted link around the current index.
nodes.section: A Details of the nonlinear FAR algorithm

nodes.name: Approximate sum of squares
nodes.statement:
Thus, we can approximate (\ref{etaopt}) as


\begin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^n
\Biggl(R_i - \sum_{j=1}^p
{\mathbf h}'\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}
\bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j \cdot\bolds\theta_{ij}^T(
\bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}) \Biggr)^2,
\end{equation}

where\vspace*{1pt} $R_i = Y_i - \sum_{j=1}^p {\mathbf h}(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta
_{j,\mathrm{old}})^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j $, that is, the residual for the $i$th observation
from step~2 of the algorithm in the current iteration.
nodes.statement_short: Form the linearized least-squares objective with residuals R_i.

nodes.name: Minimize quadratic
nodes.statement:
The above
approximation (\ref{etaoptapprox}) is a quadratic function of $\bolds\eta
_j$ and can be minimized easily. Hence, the new value of $\bolds\eta_j$ is
updated as the minimizer of (\ref{etaoptapprox}).
nodes.statement_short: Update index as minimizer of the quadratic approximation.

nodes.name: Skip zero links
nodes.statement:
We also note that if
the estimate $\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$ from step~2 is $\mathbf{0}$, then the
corresponding value of $\bolds\eta_j$ will not be updated.
nodes.statement_short: Do not update the index when the link coefficients are zero.

nodes.statement:

\bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j\approx{\mathbf h}\bigl(\bolds\theta

nodes.name: Condition 1 (Sobolev predictors and bounded coefficients)
nodes.statement:
\textup{(A)} Functional predictors, $\{X_{ij}:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R},
i=1,\ldots,n, \break j=1,\ldots,{p_n}\}$, belong to a Sobolev ellipsoid of
order two: there exists a universal constant $C$, such that $\sum
_{k=1}^{\infty} \theta^2_{ijk}k^4\le C^2$ for all $i=1,\ldots,n,
j=1,\ldots,{p_n}$.

(B) The true coefficient functions satisfy $\max_{ j\in\mathfrak{M}
_0}\int_0^1\beta^2_j(t)\,dt \leq\widetilde C$ with $\widetilde C$ some
positive constant.
nodes.statement_short: Predictors lie in an order-two Sobolev ellipsoid; true coefficient functions have bounded L2 norm.
nodes.label: as3

nodes.name: Linear FAR model in basis form
nodes.statement:
Y_i = \sum_{j=1}^p
\Theta_{j}\bolds\eta_j + \varepsilon_i^*,
nodes.label: linearapprox

nodes.name: Argument for the total approximation error bound
nodes.statement:
When $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c$, $\beta_j(t)=0$ and thus the approximation
error $e_{ij}$ in (\ref{fexpan}) disappears.
nodes.statement_short: Noise predictors contribute no approximation error, so sum the per-signal bound.

nodes.name: Total approximation error bound
Condition 2 (penalty shape, signal strength, design, errors)
nodes.statement:
(A) For any fixed $\lambda>0$, $\rho_{\lambda}(t)$ is
concave and nondecreasing in $[0, \infty)$, and has nonincreasing
first derivative
$\rho_{\lambda}'(t)$. Further, $\rho'_\lambda(0+)>0$.

(B) Let $a_n=\min_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0}\Vert \Theta_j\bolds\eta
_{0,j}\Vert
/\sqrt{n}$. It holds that $n^{\alpha} a_n \rightarrow\infty$ with
$\alpha\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$.

(C) It holds that $\rho'_{\lambda_n}(a_n/2)=o (n^{-\alpha
}q_n^{-1}s_n^{-1/2} )$ and $\sup_{t\geq\sfrac{a_n}{2}}\rho
''_{\lambda_n}(t)=o(1)$.

(D) There exists a positive constant $c_0$ such that


\begin{equation} c_0\leq\min_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0}
\Lambda_{\min}\biggl(\frac{1}{n} \Theta_{j}^T
\Theta_{j}\biggr)<\Lambda_{\max}\biggl(\frac{1}{n}
\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}\biggr)\leq
c_0^{-1},
\end{equation}

where $\Lambda_{\min}$ and $\Lambda_{\max}$
are the smallest and largest eigenvalues of a matrix, respectively.
Further, we have


\begin{eqnarray} && \max_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\Theta_j
\bigl(\Theta_j^T\Theta_j
\bigr)^{-1}\Theta_j^T \Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}
\bigl(\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}
\bigr)^{-1} \bigr\Vert_{\infty,
2}<\frac{\sqrt{c_0}}{2\sqrt{n}}
\frac{\rho'_{\lambda_n}(0+)}{\rho
'_{\lambda_n}(a_n/2)},




\end{eqnarray}

where for a matrix $B$, $\Vert B\Vert _{\infty,2} = \sup
_{\Vert {\mathbf x}\Vert
_\infty=1}\Vert B{\mathbf x}\Vert _2$ with ${\mathbf x}$ a vector.


(E) The model errors $\varepsilon_i$, $i=1,\ldots, n$ are
independent and identically distributed as $N(0,\sigma^2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Concave singular penalty, signal decaying no faster than n^{-alpha}, flat penalty tails, bounded eigenvalues with irrepresentability-type bound, Gaussian errors.
nodes.label: as2

nodes.name: Eigenvalue bounds for signal design
nodes.label: eqeigen

nodes.name: Irrepresentable-type condition for noise predictors
nodes.label: e015

nodes.name: Discussion of Condition 2
nodes.statement:
Condition~\ref{as2}(A) requires that the penalty functional, $\rho
_{\lambda}(t)$, is concave and singular at 0. Many penalty functions
proposed in the literature such as the hard thresholding penalty, SCAD
\cite{fan2} and SICA \cite{lv1} all satisfy this condition. From
(\ref{fexpan}), we see that Condition~\ref{as2}(B)
places a lower bound on the signal strength of the true predictors
$j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$. In particular, it assumes that the weakest signal,
$a_n$, can decay with sample
size but the decay rate cannot be faster than $n^{-\alpha}$. Condition
\ref{as2}(C) is a mild condition which can be easily satisfied by
penalty functions with flat tails. For instance, if $\lambda_n =
o(a_n/2)$, then for SCAD penalty, it can be verified from the
definition that $\rho'_{\lambda_n}(a_n/2) = 0$ and $\rho''_{\lambda
_n}(t) = 0$ for all $t \geq a_n/2$, and thus\vspace*{1pt} Condition~\ref{as2}(C) is
satisfied. Although Condition~\ref{as2}(C) assumes the existence of
the second-order derivative for
$\rho_{\lambda_n}(t)$, it can be relaxed to the existence of the
first-order derivative by using the local concavity definition in \cite
{lv1}. Condition~\ref{as2}(D)
relates to the design matrix for the signal predictors, $\Theta
_{\mathfrak{M}_0}$. We assume that the eigenvalues for the design matrix
corresponding to true predictors
are bounded from below and above. If $\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}$ is
orthogonal, then (\ref{eqeigen}) is satisfied with $c_0 = 1$. The
upper bound in condition (\ref{e015}) depends on the penalty function
through the ratio
$\rho'_{\lambda_n}(0+)/\rho_{\lambda_n}'(a_n/2)$, which is larger
than 1 for concave penalties and equal to 1 for the group Lasso penalty,
$\rho_{\lambda_n}(t)=\lambda_n t$. For instance, if $\lambda_n =
o(a_n)$, then $\rho'_{\lambda_n}(0+)/\rho_{\lambda_n}'(a_n/2) =
\infty$ for SCAD penalty and thus (\ref{e015}) is satisfied
automatically.
nodes.statement_short: Common concave penalties (SCAD, SICA, hard thresholding) satisfy Condition 2; orthogonal design gives c_0=1; SCAD satisfies (C) and the irrepresentable bound automatically.

nodes.name: Truncated true index coefficients eta_j^*
nodes.statement:
Given an orthonormal basis expansion for $\beta_j(t)$, that is, $\beta
_j(t)=\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\eta^*_{jl}b_l(t)$, we will define $\bolds\eta
_j^*=(\eta^*_{j1},\ldots,\eta^*_{jq_n})^T$.

nodes.name: Best spline approximation f_j^*
nodes.statement:
We will also define $f_j^*(\bolds\theta_{ij})={\mathbf h}_{\bolds\eta^*_j,j}(\bolds\theta
_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*)\bolds\xi^*$, where $\bolds\xi_j^*$ is chosen to minimize
$\sum_{i=1}^n [{\mathbf h}_{\bolds\eta^*_j,j}\times\break (\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*)\bolds\xi
-g_{0j}(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*)]^2$ over~$\bolds\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d_n}$ with
the constraint $\sum_i f_j^*(\bolds\theta_{ij})=0$.

nodes.name: Condition 3 (regularity for nonlinear FAR)
nodes.statement:
(A) Functional predictors, $\{X_{ij}:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R},
i=1,\ldots,n, j=1,\ldots,{p_n}\}$, belong\vspace*{1pt} to a Sobolev ellipsoid of
order two: there exists a universal constant $C$, such that $\sum
_{k=1}^{\infty} \theta^2_{ijk}k^4\le C^2$ for all $i=1,\ldots,n,
j=1,\ldots,{p_n}$.

(B) The true index functions, $\{\beta_j(t), j\in\mathfrak{M}_0\}
$, satisfy $\int_0^1\beta^2_j(t)\,dt=1$.

(C) Errors~$\varepsilon_i$ are independent and uniformly
sub-Gaussian.

(D) The true link functions, $g_{0j}$, are twice continuously
differentiable and are bounded, together with their first and second
derivatives, uniformly over~$j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$ and~$n$.

(E) For\vspace*{1pt} each $\bolds\eta$ with $\Vert \bolds\eta\Vert =1$ and each
$j\le
{p_n}$ let~$Q_{\bolds\eta,j,n}$ denote the empirical distribution
associated with the index values $\bolds\eta^T\bolds\theta_{1j},\ldots,
\bolds\eta^T\bolds\theta_{nj}$. Assume that there exist corresponding
probability distributions~$P_{\bolds\eta,j,n}$, each with bounded support
and a positive continuous density, such that the densities are bounded
both above and away from zero uniformly over $j$ and $n$, and


\begin{equation}
\sup_{u\in\mathbb{R}, \Vert \bolds\eta\Vert =1, 1\le j\le{p_n}}\bigl\vert
Q_{\bolds\eta
,j,n}(-
\infty,u]-P_{\bolds\eta,j,n}(-\infty,u]\bigr\vert=o \bigl(d_n^{-1}
\bigr).
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Sobolev predictors, unit-norm index functions, sub-Gaussian errors, smooth bounded links, and regular index-value distributions.
nodes.label: cond3

nodes.name: Uniform closeness of empirical index distributions
nodes.statement:
\sup_{u\in\mathbb{R}, \Vert \bolds\eta\Vert =1, 1\le j\le{p_n}}\bigl\vert
Q_{\bolds\eta
,j,n}(-
\infty,u]-P_{\bolds\eta,j,n}(-\infty,u]\bigr\vert=o \bigl(d_n^{-1}
\bigr).

nodes.name: Discussion of Condition 3
nodes.statement:
Condition~\ref{cond3}(A) is identical to Condition~\ref{as3}(A),
imposed for the linear FAR theory. It is a common smoothness
requirement in nonparametric regression, when the orthogonal basis
approach is used, as discussed, for example, in Chapter~8 in \cite
{Bwasserman1}. Condition~\ref{cond3}(B) is imposed for
identifiability. Conditions~\ref{cond3}(C) and~(D) are typical in
high-dimensional regression and nonparametric regression problems,
respectively. The reason we require uniformity is to handle the
situation where the number of signal predictors grows with~$n$. Again,
uniformity is needed to handle the growing number of signal predictors.\vspace*{1pt}
Condition~\ref{cond3}(E) ensures that the candidate index values,
$\bolds\eta^T\bolds\theta_{1j},\ldots, \bolds\eta^T\bolds\theta_{nj}$, have
sufficiently regular distributions. Assumptions of this form are
typical in spline estimation \cite{zhou2}, for example.

nodes.name: Discussion of Condition 4
nodes.statement:
We impose two more assumptions below. Condition~\ref{as4}(A) is a
natural generalization of the \emph{compatibility condition} used in
high-dimensional additive models, for example, in \cite{meier1} and
Section~8.4. in \cite{Bbuhlmann1}. Note that because we do not use a
smoothness penalty in our estimation approach, the smoothness penalty
does not appear in the compatibility condition. Condition~\ref{as4}(B)
is a version of the standard regularity condition on the behavior of
the sum of squares function near its minimum. Assumptions of this form
have been imposed in the single index model literature, for example,
\cite{yu1}. We again require uniformity over $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$ to
handle the growing number of signal predictors.

nodes.name: Condition 4 (compatibility and index regularity)
nodes.statement:
(A) There exists a positive universal constant $\phi^2$ for
which the following holds. If functions $\{h_j, j=1,\ldots,{p_n}\}$
are such that each $h_j$ is a difference of two functions in ${\mathcal F}_j^0$,
and inequality $\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c}\Vert h_{j}\Vert _n\le3\sum
_{j\in
\mathfrak{M}_0}\Vert h_{j}\Vert _n$ is satisfied, then the following inequality
holds: $\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0}\Vert h_{j}\Vert _n^2\le\Vert \sum
_{j=1}^{{p_n}}h_j\Vert ^2_n/\phi^2$.

(B) There exist positive universal constants $\tau$, $c_1$ and
$c_2$, such that for all sufficiently large~$n$ and each $f_{\bolds\eta
_j,j}(\cdot)={\mathbf h}_{\bolds\eta_j,j}(\bolds\eta_j^T\cdot)\bolds\xi$ with~$\Vert
\bolds\eta_j\Vert =\Vert \bolds\eta_j^*\Vert $ and $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$,
inequalities $\Vert
f_{\bolds\eta_j,j} - f^*_j\Vert _n\le\tau$ and $\Vert \bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta
_j^*\Vert <\Vert
\bolds\eta_j+\bolds\eta_j^*\Vert $ imply $\Vert \bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta
_j^*\Vert \le c_1\Vert
f_{\bolds\eta_j,j} - f^*_j\Vert _n$ and $\Vert f_{\bolds\eta_j^*,j} -
f^*_j\Vert _n\le
c_2\Vert f_{\bolds\eta_j,j} - f^*_j\Vert _n$.
nodes.statement_short: Compatibility condition for additive components and local identifiability of the index near the truth.
nodes.label: as4

nodes.name: Approximation error bound for index and link
nodes.statement:
We start by deriving a bound on the error due to our approximation of
index functions~$\beta_j$ and link functions~$g_{0j}$. Observe that

\begin{eqnarray*}
\biggl\vert\int_0^1\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt
- \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*\biggr\vert
^2&=&\Biggl\vert\sum_{k=q_n+1}^{\infty}
\eta^*_{jk}k^{-2}k^2\theta_{ijk}\Biggr
\vert^2
\\
&\le&\sum_{k=q_n+1}^{\infty}\bigl(
\eta^*_{jk}\bigr)^2k^{-4}\sum
_{k=q_n+1}^{\infty}\theta^2_{ijk}k^{-4}.
\end{eqnarray*}

Condition~\ref{cond3}(A) implies that the right-most sum is bounded by
a universal constant~$C^2$. Also\vspace*{1pt} note that $\sum_{l=q_n+1}^{\infty
}(\eta_{jl}^*)^2k^{-4}\le q_n^{-4}\sum_{k=q_n+1}^{\infty}(\eta
_{jk}^*)^2\le q_n^{-4}$, by Condition~\ref{cond3}(B). Thus, if we set
$I_{ij}=\int_0^1\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt$, then the bound $\vert I_{ij} -
\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*\vert \le Cq_n^{-2}$ holds for all $n$, $i$, and
$j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$.
Hence, if we let $\widetilde C$ be the uniform bound over the first
derivatives in Condition~\ref{cond3}(D), then


\begin{equation} \bigl\vert g_{0j}(I_{ij}) -
g_{0j} \bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*
\bigr)\bigr\vert\le\widetilde C\bigl\vert I_{ij} -
\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*\bigr\vert= O
\bigl(q_n^{-2}\bigr),
\end{equation}

uniformly over $i$ and $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$. Set $M_j=\sup_t\vert g^{\prime
\prime}_{0j}(t)\vert $ for $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$, and note that constants $M_j$
are uniformly bounded by Condition~\ref{cond3}(D). Taking advantage of
the approximation bounds for the cubic B-splines (e.g., Corollary~6.21
in \cite{BSchumaker1}), we then have


\begin{equation} n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n
\bigl(g_{0j} \bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T
\bolds\eta_j^* \bigr)-f^*_j(\bolds\theta_{ij})
\bigr)^2=O\bigl(d_n^{-4}M_j^2
\bigr)=O\bigl(d_n^{-4}\bigr),
\end{equation}

uniformly over $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$. Combining inequalities~(\ref
{prelimappr1}) and~(\ref{prelimappr2}), we deduce
$\Vert f_{0j}-f_{j}^*\Vert _n=O(q_n^{-2}+d_n^{-2})=O(d_n^{-2})$,
uniformly over $j$.
Note that for $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c$, both $f_{0j}$ and $f_{j}^*$ are zero.
Consequently,


\begin{equation} \sum_{j=1}^{{p_n}}\bigl\Vert
f_j^*-f_{0j}\bigr\Vert_n=O
\bigl(s_nd_n^{-2}\bigr).
\end{equation}

This gives us a useful bound on the approximation error.
nodes.statement_short: Sobolev condition plus B-spline approximation give summed approximation error O(s_n d_n^{-2}).

nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Additive sum notation
nodes.statement:
We will write~$f_0({\mathbf X}_i)$ for $\sum_{j=1}^{{p_n}} f_{0j}(X_{ij})$;
we also write~$\hat f(\bolds\theta_i)$ for $\sum_{j=1}^{{p_n}}\hat f_j(\bolds\theta_{ij})$ and define $f^*$ by analogy.

nodes.name: Empirical inner product with noise
nodes.statement:
To be consistent with
the standard least-squares estimation notation, we will
write~$(\varepsilon,f)_n$ for $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i
f(\bolds\theta_{i})$.

nodes.name: Empirical process bound
nodes.statement:
Define $r_n=n^{-1/2}q_n^{1/2}+n^{-1/2}\sqrt{\log{p_n}}$.
There exists a positive universal constant $C_1$, such that


\begin{equation}
\bigl(\varepsilon,\hat f-f^*\bigr)_n\le C_1s_nr_n^2+C_1r_n
\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n,
\end{equation}

with probability tending to one.
nodes.statement_short: The noise cross term is bounded by C_1 s_n r_n^2 plus C_1 r_n times the summed component errors.

\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n,

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement:
Let $\Vert y-f\Vert ^2_n$ denote $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-f(\bolds\theta
_{i}))^2$
and let $\Vert f\Vert ^2_n$ denote $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(\bolds\theta_{i})^2$.
Consider the following simple identity:


\begin{equation} \Vert y-\hat f\Vert_n^2-\bigl
\Vert y-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2=\Vert\hat f-f_0\Vert_n^2-\bigl\Vert
f^*-f_0\bigr\Vert_n^2-2\bigl(\varepsilon,
\hat f - f^*\bigr)_n.
\end{equation}

Note that $\Vert y-\hat f\Vert _n^2+\lambda_n\sum
_{j=1}^{p_n}\Vert \hat f_j\Vert _n-\Vert y-f^*\Vert _n^2-\lambda_n\sum
_{j=1}^{p_n}\Vert f_j^*\Vert _n\le0$ by
the definition of~$\hat f$. Let~$e_n$ denote the approximation
error, $\Vert f^* - f_0\Vert _n$. Inequality~(\ref{basicineq1})
then implies

\[
\Vert\hat f-f_0\Vert_n^2+
\lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\Vert
\hat f_j\Vert_n\le e_n^2+2
\bigl(\varepsilon,\hat f - f^*\bigr)_n+\lambda_n\sum
_{j=1}^{p_n}\bigl\Vert f_j^*
\bigr\Vert_n.
\]

By Lemma~\ref{lementrcons}, the above inequality yields


\begin{eqnarray} && \Vert\hat f-f_0\Vert_n^2+
\lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\Vert
\hat f_j\Vert_n
\nonumber\\[-10pt]\\[-10pt]\nonumber
&&\qquad \le e_n^2+2C_1s_nr_n^2+2C_1r_n
\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+
\lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\bigl
\Vert f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n,
\end{eqnarray}

with probability tending to one.

\begin{longlist}
\item[\textit{Case} (i).]
Consider the event $e_n^2+C_1s_nr_n^2\ge r_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert
\hat f_j-f_j^*\Vert _n$.

Note that $e_n^2=O(s_n^2d_n^{-4})$ by~(\ref{approxbnd}).
Thus, $\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_j^*\Vert _n =
O(s_n^2n^{1/2}d_n^{-4}\*q_n^{-1/2}+s_nr_n)$. Consequently,
$\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert
_n=O(d_n^{-4}q_n^{-1/2}+s_nr_n+s_nd_n^{-2})$, which implies the
stochastic bound in display~(\ref{nonlinthmbnd}).\vspace*{1pt}

\item[\textit{Case} (ii).]
Consider the event $e_n^2+C_1s_nr_n^2< r_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert
\hat f_j-f_j^*\Vert _n$.\vadjust{\goodbreak}

Using inequality $\Vert \hat f-f^*\Vert ^2_n\le
2\Vert \hat f-f_0\Vert _n^2 +2e_n^2$ together with~(\ref{basicineq1b}), we get

\begin{eqnarray*}
&& \bigl\Vert\hat f-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2+2
\lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert
\hat f_j\Vert_n
\\
&&\qquad \le4e_n^2+4C_1s_nr_n^2+4C_1r_n
\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+2
\lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl
\Vert f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n.
\end{eqnarray*}

On the event $e_n^2+C_1s_nr_n^2< r_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_j^*\Vert _n$ the above inequality simplifies to


\begin{eqnarray} && \bigl\Vert\hat f-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2+2
\lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert
\hat f_j\Vert_n
\nonumber\\[-8pt]\\[-8pt]\nonumber
&&\qquad \le4(C_1+1)r_n
\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+2\lambda
_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert
f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n.
\end{eqnarray}

Because we assume $r_n=O(\lambda_n)$, we can rewrite inequality~(\ref
{basicineq3}) as


\begin{equation} \bigl\Vert\hat f-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2
= \sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f^*_j\bigr\Vert_n O(
\lambda_n).
\end{equation}

Inequality~(\ref{basicineq3}) also gives

\[
\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \Vert\hat f_j\Vert
_n\le2\lambda_n^{-1}(C_1+1)r_n
\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+\sum
_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*
\bigr\Vert_n.
\]

Consequently,

\begin{eqnarray*}
\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n
&\le& 2\lambda
_n^{-1}(C_1+1)r_n\sum
_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*
\bigr\Vert_n
\\
&&{} +\bigl[2\lambda_n^{-1}(C_1+1)r_n+1
\bigr]\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n,
\end{eqnarray*}

which, provided $\lambda_n\ge4(C_1+1)r_n$, implies


\begin{equation} \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n\le3\sum
_{j\in
\mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*
\bigr\Vert_n.
\end{equation}

This allows us to apply the compatibility condition,~\ref{as4}(A), to
$\hat f -f^*$. It follows that $s_n^{-1}(\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \Vert
\hat f_j-f^*_j\Vert _n)^2\le\Vert \hat f-f^*\Vert
_n^2/\phi^2$, which,
by~(\ref{compatbnd}), yields $s_n^{-1}(\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert
\hat f_j-f^*_j\Vert _n)^2\le16\Vert \hat f-f^*\Vert _n^2/\phi
^2$. Stochastic
bound~(\ref{stochbndlam}) then gives $\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f^*_j\Vert _n= O(s_n\lambda_n)$, and\vspace*{2pt} hence $\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}
\Vert
\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert _n= O(s_n\lambda_n+s_nd_n^{-2})$, which again
implies the bound in display~(\ref{nonlinthmbnd}). This completes
the proof of Theorem~\ref{nonlinthm}.

nodes.statement:

\[
\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \Vert\hat f_j\Vert
_n\le2\lambda_n^{-1}(C_1+1)r_n
\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+\sum
_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*
\bigr\Vert_n.
\]

Consequently,

\begin{eqnarray*}
\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n
&\le& 2\lambda
_n^{-1}(C_1+1)r_n\sum
_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*
\bigr\Vert_n
\\
&&{} +\bigl[2\lambda_n^{-1}(C_1+1)r_n+1
\bigr]\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n,
\end{eqnarray*}

which, provided $\lambda_n\ge4(C_1+1)r_n$, implies


\begin{equation} \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n\le3\sum
_{j\in
\mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*
\bigr\Vert_n.
\end{equation}

$\hat f -f^*$. It follows that $s_n^{-1}(\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \Vert
\hat f_j-f^*_j\Vert _n)^2\le\Vert \hat f-f^*\Vert
_n^2/\phi^2$, which,
by~(\ref{compatbnd}), yields $s_n^{-1}(\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert
\hat f_j-f^*_j\Vert _n)^2\le16\Vert \hat f-f^*\Vert _n^2/\phi
^2$.

bound~(\ref{stochbndlam}) then gives $\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f^*_j\Vert _n= O(s_n\lambda_n)$, and\vspace*{2pt} hence $\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}
\Vert
\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert _n= O(s_n\lambda_n+s_nd_n^{-2})$, which again
implies the bound in display~(\ref{nonlinthmbnd}). This completes
the proof of Theorem~\ref{nonlinthm}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement:
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{threshthm}, the error bound in
the statement of Theorem~\ref{nonlinthm} simplifies to $\sum
_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert _n=O(s_n\lambda_n)$.
Consequently,
on the sets of probability tending to one,


\begin{equation} \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \Vert\tilde f_j\Vert_n\le\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}
_0^c}
\Vert\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert_n=O(s_n
\lambda_n).
\end{equation}

Using bound~(\ref{bndprfthrthm}) and the fact that $\Vert \tilde f_j\Vert _n>\lambda_n$ for $j\in\widetilde\mathfrak{M}_n$, we can deduce
$\vert \mathfrak{M}_0^c\cap\widetilde\mathfrak{M}_n\vert =O(s_n)$. This implies
$\vert \widetilde\mathfrak{M}_n\vert \le\vert \mathfrak{M}_0\vert
+\vert \mathfrak{M}_0^c\cap\widetilde
\mathfrak{M}_n\vert =O(s_n)$.
Also note that

\[
\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \Vert\tilde f_j-f_{0j}
\Vert_n\le\sum_{j\in
\mathfrak{M}_0}\bigl(
\lambda_n+ \Vert\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert
_n\bigr) =O(s_n\lambda_n).
\]

The above bound, together with~(\ref{bndprfthrthm}), yields the
error bound in Theorem~\ref{threshthm}.

nodes.name: Initialize
Partial residual
nodes.statement:
[1.] Fix all $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_k$ for $k\ne j$. Compute the residual vector
${\mathbf R}_j = {\mathbf Y}-
\sum_{k\ne j} \hat{{\mathbf f}}_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix other components and form the partial residual.

nodes.name: Unshrunk estimate
nodes.statement:
[2.] Let $\widehat{\mathbf P}_j = S_j {\mathbf R}_j$ represent the unshrunk
estimate for ${\mathbf f}_j$.\vspace*{2pt}
nodes.statement_short: Project residual onto predictor j's basis span.

nodes.name: Group soft-threshold
nodes.statement_short: Shrink the projection by the group soft-threshold factor.

nodes.name: Center
nodes.statement: [4.] Center $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j \leftarrow\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j - \operatorname{mean}(\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j)$.\vspace*{2pt}

nodes.name: Cycle until convergence
nodes.statement:
[5.] Repeat steps~1 through 4 for $j=1,2,\ldots, p$ and iterate until
convergence.
nodes.statement_short: Cycle over predictors until convergence.

nodes.name: Initialize via linear FAR
nodes.statement:
[0.] Initialize\vspace*{2pt}~$\hat{\bolds\eta}_j$ for $j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$
using the linear FAR algorithm.
nodes.statement_short: Initialize index vectors with the linear FAR fit.

nodes.name: Compute H_j
nodes.statement: [1.] Compute $\widehat H_j$ using the current estimates for $\bolds\eta_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Build spline design matrices from current indices.

nodes.name: Estimate link coefficients
nodes.statement:
[2.] Estimate $\bolds\xi_j$ for $j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$ by minimizing
(\ref{nonlinfar2}) given the current values of $\widehat H_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Penalized fit of link coefficients given H_j.

nodes.name: Estimate index vectors
nodes.statement:
[3.] Conditional on the $\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$'s from step~2, estimate the
$\bolds\eta_j$'s by minimizing (\ref{etaopt}).
nodes.statement_short: Least-squares update of index vectors given link coefficients.

nodes.name: Iterate
nodes.statement: [4.] Repeat steps 1~through 3 and iterate until convergence.
nodes.statement_short: Alternate steps 1-3 until convergence.
